title: Complete Faucet Checklist for a New Bathroom: Pillar Tap, Bib Cock, Angle Cock, Wall Mixer, Diverter and Spout
metaTitle: Complete Faucet Checklist for a New Bathroom | Prayag
description: Use this complete bathroom faucet checklist to plan pillar taps, bib cocks, angle cocks, wall mixers, diverters and spouts without missing fittings.
bodyHtml:
Quick answer

A complete faucet checklist for a new bathroom should begin with the room layout, not the finish catalogue. Count every water point, confirm which fittings will be concealed or exposed, match each faucet to the basin, shower and utility requirement, and leave enough access for future servicing. A typical bathroom may need a pillar tap or basin mixer, one or more angle cocks, a bib cock, a wall mixer or diverter, a bath spout, a health faucet and supporting accessories. The exact combination depends on the plumbing plan and daily use pattern.

The safest approach is to freeze the specification before tiles and walls are closed. Buyers can compare active product families on the Prayag Faucets page, but the final selection should be checked against actual pipe positions, pressure conditions, mounting clearances and finish consistency.

Why a room-by-room faucet checklist matters

A bathroom often looks like one small room, but it contains several independent water points. The wash basin, shower area, toilet, geyser line and cleaning point may each need a different fitting. Missing even one angle cock or choosing the wrong diverter body can delay installation because the plumber cannot complete the connection after tiles, counters or cabinets are fixed.

A written checklist also prevents last-minute substitutions. When products are purchased in stages without a common specification, finishes may not match, handle shapes may change, and service parts may come from unrelated families. Standardising visible fittings makes the bathroom look more deliberate and usually makes maintenance easier later.

Complete Bathroom Faucet Checklist

FittingTypical locationMain jobCheck before buying
Pillar tap or basin mixerWash basin counterSupplies water for handwashingBasin hole, spout reach, spout height and hot/cold line requirement
Angle cockBelow basin, cistern, geyser or health faucetIsolates supply to one fixtureThread size, outlet direction, handle clearance and shut-off quality
Bib cockLow wall outlet, utility point or balconyProvides a direct wall-mounted water outletWall outlet height, hose requirement, reach and splash area
Wall mixerShower or bath areaMixes hot and cold water and sends it to shower or spoutInlet spacing, pressure balance, shower connection and service access
Concealed diverterBehind shower wallControls mixed water and switches flow between outletsBody depth, number of outlets, flow demand and concealed installation stage
Bath spoutBelow mixer or diverterDelivers water into the bathing area or bucketProjection, wall height, diverter compatibility and splash direction
Health faucetBeside WCSupports personal cleaningHose length, trigger quality, pressure and accessible angle cock

1. Basin area: pillar tap, basin mixer or wall-mounted faucet

Start with the basin type. A deck-mounted pillar tap fits a basin or counter with a suitable tap hole and a single water line. A basin mixer is more appropriate when hot and cold water must be controlled at one point. A wall-mounted faucet can free up counter space, but its concealed outlet position must be fixed accurately before tiling.

Measure basin width, bowl depth, faucet height and reach together. Water should land close to the drain rather than hitting the near rim. For vessel or countertop basins, use the guidance in the countertop wash basin faucet selection guide. A faucet that is too tall for a shallow bowl can create constant splash, while a short spout may force users to wash their hands close to the basin edge.

2. Angle cocks: count every isolation point

Angle cocks are easy to overlook because they are small, but they are among the most important service fittings in the bathroom. They allow one fixture to be shut off without stopping water to the entire room or house. Common locations include the basin mixer, WC cistern, health faucet and geyser connections.

Count the hot and cold lines separately. A basin mixer usually needs two angle cocks, while a single-line pillar tap may need one. The WC cistern and health faucet generally need their own supply control. Keep the handle reachable after the vanity, bottle trap and cabinet are installed. A hidden angle cock may technically work but becomes frustrating when a washer, hose or fixture needs replacement.

3. Bib cock: utility, cleaning and direct wall outlet

A bib cock provides a direct wall-mounted outlet and is commonly used for bucket filling, floor cleaning, balcony washing or a washing-machine utility point. Choose the outlet height based on how it will be used. A low outlet may be convenient for bucket filling but difficult to connect to a hose if the surrounding clearance is poor.

When comparing bib cocks with angle cocks and stop cocks, review the bib cock vs angle cock vs stop cock guide. These fittings may look related, but they perform different jobs. A bib cock is a usable outlet, while an angle cock primarily controls supply to another fixture.

4. Wall mixer: exposed control for hot and cold water

A wall mixer is a practical option when the hot and cold inlets remain visible and the buyer wants direct control without a concealed body. Depending on the model, it may feed a hand shower, overhead shower or bath spout. Installation is simpler to inspect than a concealed diverter, but inlet spacing and wall alignment must be accurate for a neat result.

Check whether water pressure is reasonably balanced on both hot and cold lines. Very different pressures can make temperature control inconsistent. The mixer should also match the intended shower outlet and spout arrangement. Do not assume that every wall mixer supports every combination of outlets.

5. Concealed diverter: plan before closing the wall

A concealed diverter gives the shower area a cleaner appearance because the valve body remains behind the wall. It mixes hot and cold water and directs the flow to selected outlets, such as an overhead shower, hand shower or bath spout. The decision between an exposed wall mixer and a concealed diverter should be made before plumbing and tiling are finalised. The diverter versus wall mixer guide explains the practical difference in layout and use.

Confirm the diverter body depth, number of outlets and flow requirement. A high-flow shower system may need a different body from a basic two-outlet setup. The concealed body must be installed level, at the correct depth and with access to replace the cartridge or operating parts from the front. If the body is set too deep or too shallow, the external trim may not sit properly after tiling.

6. Spout: projection and outlet position matter

The bath spout is not only a decorative extension. Its projection determines where water lands, and its mounting height affects bucket filling and splash. Check whether the selected spout includes a tip-ton arrangement or whether flow switching is handled entirely through the diverter. The spout finish should match the mixer or diverter trim because these products are seen together.

Avoid placing the spout too close to a ledge or too high above the floor. Test the expected bucket or bathing position on site. A spout that looks proportionate on a display board may feel short when installed over a deep ledge or broad tile projection.

7. Water pressure, cartridge and flow checks

Before finalising the set, confirm the expected water pressure. Low pressure can weaken shower performance, while excessive pressure may increase noise, splash and stress on hoses or seals. The faucet water-pressure guide can help buyers understand why the same faucet may behave differently across floors, homes and supply systems.

Cartridge and spindle quality influence how smoothly the fitting operates and how well it shuts off. Aerators should produce a controlled stream without excessive side spray. In hard-water areas, mineral deposits can affect aerators, cartridges and visible finishes, so regular cleaning and suitable product selection become more important.

For locations with mineral-heavy supply, review the guide to choosing faucets for hard-water areas. This helps set realistic maintenance expectations before the entire bathroom set is purchased.

Finish consistency and product-family planning

Visible fittings should ideally come from one coordinated finish family. Chrome from two unrelated product lines can differ slightly in tone, reflection and handle shape. Matte or coloured finishes make these differences even more noticeable. Select the main shower control first, then coordinate the basin faucet, bib cock, angle cocks, spout and accessories around it.

Contractors and homeowners should keep product codes in the final purchase sheet rather than relying only on generic names. “One angle cock” is not specific enough when multiple handle designs and finishes are available. Product codes reduce substitution errors and help the dealer supply matching components.

Site-ready quantity checklist

  1. Number of wash basins and whether each needs a pillar tap, basin mixer or wall-mounted faucet.

  2. Number of hot and cold angle cocks below every basin mixer.

  3. Separate angle cocks for WC cisterns, health faucets and geyser connections.

  4. Bib cocks required for bucket filling, floor cleaning, balcony or utility use.

  5. Wall mixer or concealed diverter required for each shower area.

  6. Number of shower outlets: overhead shower, hand shower, body shower or bath spout.

  7. Bath spout type, projection and whether a flow-switching feature is needed.

  8. Health faucet, hose, holder and accessible control valve.

  9. Bottle traps, waste couplings, connection hoses and other supporting fittings.

  10. Final finish, product codes and spare quantity for multi-bathroom projects.

Mistakes to avoid before installation

  1. Buying visible products first and checking concealed plumbing later.

  2. Forgetting to count separate hot and cold angle cocks.

  3. Choosing a diverter without confirming the number of shower outlets.

  4. Ignoring basin dimensions while selecting faucet height and reach.

  5. Mixing finishes from unrelated product families.

  6. Closing the wall without testing concealed joints and valve operation.

  7. Leaving no access for cartridge, hose or angle-cock replacement.

  8. Approving the lowest quotation without checking product codes and included fittings.

Frequently asked questions

How many angle cocks are needed in one bathroom?

The number depends on the layout. Count each controlled supply point separately. A hot-and-cold basin mixer may need two, while the WC cistern, health faucet and geyser connections may each need additional angle cocks.

Should I choose a wall mixer or concealed diverter?

Choose a wall mixer when visible plumbing and easier inspection suit the project. Choose a concealed diverter when a cleaner shower wall is preferred and the concealed body can be installed and tested correctly before tiling.

Do all bathrooms need a bib cock?

Not always, but a direct outlet is useful for bucket filling and cleaning. Its need depends on the room layout and whether another outlet already serves that purpose.

Should every fitting have the same finish?

Visible products should ideally be coordinated. Matching the faucet, mixer or diverter, spout, bib cock and accessories creates a cleaner result and reduces noticeable shade differences.

When should the final faucet list be approved?

Approve it before concealed plumbing is closed and before counters or basins are ordered. The plumbing plan, basin specification and shower outlet arrangement should all agree with the final product list.

Final checklist before placing the order

Walk through the bathroom point by point with the plumbing drawing and product list. Confirm quantities, hot and cold connections, mounting type, pressure suitability, finish, product codes and service access. Then verify that concealed bodies, external trims, spouts and supporting fittings are included in the same order.

Once these details are locked, compare the relevant product families on the Prayag Faucets page. For project-specific questions about fitment or product availability, use the Prayag contact page. A careful checklist at this stage prevents missing fittings, mismatched finishes and expensive changes after installation.
